verdicts.working: At C2, priorities are OH > CHO > lower chain > H; at C3, OH > upper chain > CH3 > H. In each Fischer projection, H is horizontal (toward), so the observed sense is inverted. This gives I (2S,3S), II (2R,3R), and III (2S,3R). I–II are enantiomers; the other pairs are diastereomers.

working:

In a Fischer projection, horizontal groups point towards the viewer; reverse the order when H is horizontal.

Independent check: At C2, priorities are OH > CHO > lower chain > H; at C3, OH > upper chain > CH3 > H. In each Fischer projection, H is horizontal (toward), so the observed sense is inverted. This gives I (2S,3S), II (2R,3R), and III (2S,3R). I–II are enantiomers; the other pairs are diastereomers.
solution:
At C2, priorities are $\mathrm{OH>CHO>C3\ chain>H}$; at C3, $\mathrm{OH>C2\ chain>CH_3>H}$. Since horizontal groups in a Fischer projection point towards the viewer, invert the observed order when H is horizontal.
Thus, I is $(2S,3S)$, II is $(2R,3R)$, and III is $(2S,3R)$.
I–II differ at both stereocentres and are enantiomers; I–III and II–III differ at one centre and are diastereomers.

figure.description: Draw three separate Fischer projections side by side, labeled I, II, and III. In each projection, draw a vertical carbon chain with CHO at the top, C2 at the first intersection, C3 at the second intersection, and CH3 at the bottom; use horizontal and vertical bonds at both intersections. Projection I: at both C2 and C3, put OH on the left and H on the right. Projection II: at both C2 and C3, put H on the left and OH on the right. Projection III: at C2, put OH on the left and H on the right; at C3, put H on the left and OH on the right. Keep all labels clear and do not add wedges or dashes.
